summary.text: Gene expression is the process in which the information in a gene is used to make a functional product, such as a protein or a functional RNA molecule.
It involves transcription, where the gene's sequence is copied into RNA, and for protein-coding genes that RNA is then translated into a chain of amino acids that folds into a protein.
In eukaryotes the first RNA copy must be modified before it is mature, and the nuclear membrane separating transcription from translation gives time for this.

facts.label: Gene products
facts.value: A protein or a functional RNA molecule

facts.label: The copying enzymes
facts.value: RNA polymerases add one ribonucleotide at a time

facts.label: RNA swap
facts.value: RNA uses uracil in place of thymine

facts.label: Eukaryote copiers
facts.value: Three types of RNA polymerase work in the nucleus

facts.label: Splicing
facts.value: Introns are removed and neighbouring exons are joined

items.prompt: A cell makes a protein from a protein-coding gene. Which description of the path is correct?

options.label: The protein is built first, then copied into RNA
The gene is copied into RNA, which is translated into a chain that folds
The gene is cut into amino acids, which are joined into RNA
The gene folds directly into a protein with no RNA involved

items.explain: The gene's sequence is transcribed into RNA, and for protein-coding genes that RNA is translated into a chain of amino acids that folds into a protein.

items.prompt: A bacterium can start translating an RNA while it is still being copied, but a human cell cannot. What makes the difference?

options.label: Human RNA is too long to be read in one go
Human cells have no ribosomes for protein making
Bacteria do not use RNA to make their proteins
A nuclear membrane keeps the two processes apart in human cells

items.explain: In prokaryotes transcription and translation happen together, while in eukaryotes the nuclear membrane separates them, which gives time for RNA processing.

items.prompt: One human gene can give rise to several different proteins. What process can make that possible?

options.label: Some introns or exons are kept or removed, giving different transcripts
The gene is rewritten into new letters each time it is read
Every cell contains several copies of the gene, each slightly different
The polymerase swaps thymine for adenine at random

items.explain: In alternative splicing, some introns or exons are either removed or retained, creating different transcripts from a single gene that can be translated into different proteins.

items.prompt: A researcher finds a gene whose RNA is never made into a protein, yet the cell clearly needs it. Is that possible?

options.label: No, because every gene must end in a protein
No, because RNA can only be a temporary copy
Yes, because for non-coding genes the finished RNA does the job itself
Yes, but only if the RNA is first turned back into DNA

items.explain: For non-coding genes, the resulting RNA itself serves a functional role in the cell, and for some the mature RNA is the final gene product.

items.prompt: In a eukaryotic cell, an enzyme adds a special cap to one end of a fresh RNA copy and a long tail of adenines to the other end. What do these additions do?

options.label: They shorten the RNA so it can leave the nucleus
They protect the RNA from being broken down
They turn the RNA into DNA
They set which amino acid comes first in the protein

items.explain: The 5′ cap and the poly(A) tail each protect the RNA from degradation.

items.prompt: A student says eukaryotic cells copy all their genes with one kind of RNA polymerase, just like bacteria do. Is the student right?

options.label: Yes, all living cells share a single polymerase
Yes, but only for protein-coding genes
No, because bacteria use three and eukaryotes use one
No, because eukaryotes use three types in the nucleus; bacteria use one

items.explain: Bacteria use a single type of RNA polymerase, while eukaryotes use three types in the nucleus.
